title: Quickselect: Kth Largest Element
oneLiner: Find the k-th largest value without sorting: partition like quicksort, then continue only into the side that holds the answer. O(n) on average.
keyTakeaway: The k-th largest is the element that would sit at index n - k after sorting. Partition puts one pivot exactly where it belongs; if that index is n - k you are done, otherwise recurse into only the side containing n - k. Throwing away half the range each round gives n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(n) on average.
explanation:
Return the k-th largest element of nums (1-based, so k = 1 is the maximum). Duplicates count: in [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6] the 4th largest is 4 (6, 5, 5, 4). Sorting and reading index n - k is O(n log n). A min-heap of size k (Top K with a Heap) is O(n log k). Quickselect is O(n) on average.

In ascending sorted order the k-th largest sits at index target = n - k. Partition the whole array around a pivot (Lomuto, with the middle element swapped to the end first). The pivot lands at its final sorted index p. If p == target, the pivot is the answer. If p < target, the answer is to the right, so repeat on [p + 1, hi]. If p > target, repeat on [lo, p - 1]. Unlike quicksort, you only ever continue into one side, so a loop is enough.

Each round costs the size of the current range. If pivots split roughly in half, the total is n + n/2 + n/4 + ..., which is under 2n: O(n) on average. Bad pivots every time give O(n²), the same risk as quicksort; a random or middle pivot makes that unlikely, and the median-of-medians pivot rule guarantees O(n) at the price of a large constant.

When to use which: quickselect for one answer from data you can rearrange; a size-k heap when the data streams in or must stay untouched; sorting when you need many order statistics.

The visualization finds the 2nd largest in [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4]: target index 6 - 2 = 4.

starterCode.python:
def find_kth_largest(nums, k):
    a = list(nums)
    target, lo, hi = len(a) - k, 0, len(a) - 1
    # TODO: loop: swap the middle of [lo, hi] into a[hi], Lomuto-partition
    # a[lo..hi] around a[hi] to get pivot index p. If p == target return a[p];
    # if p < target set lo = p + 1, else set hi = p - 1.
    return a[0]

visualizationSteps.message: Find the 2nd largest in [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4]. Sorted ascending, it would sit at index 6 - 2 = 4.
Partition positions 0 to 5 around 1: it lands at index 0. The target 4 is to the right, so drop the other side entirely.
Partition positions 1 to 5 around 5: it lands at index 4, the target. The 2nd largest is 5.

recognitionSignals: "K-th largest" or "k-th smallest", or the median, from an unsorted array, asked for in better than O(n log n).
Any "find the element that would be at position p if sorted" question.
gotchas: Mixing up k-th largest with k-th smallest: target index is n - k for largest, k - 1 for smallest.
Recursing into both sides turns it back into quicksort, O(n log n).
Using the last element as pivot on sorted input makes every round shrink by one: O(n²).
confusableWith: Top K with a Heap returns the k largest values and works on a stream, in O(n log k); quickselect returns one order statistic in O(n) average but needs the whole array in memory and rearranges it.
Quicksort recurses into both sides of each partition; quickselect into one.

complexity.note: On average each partition keeps about half the range: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... < 2n, so O(n). The worst case (extreme pivots every round) is O(n²). The loop itself needs O(1) extra space; this version works on a copy of the input, which is O(n).
